A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 20-page versions of the same SSA-COMET/SSA-MTE study, including Appendices A–J. Text, tables, figures and model descriptions can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original human-annotation agreement, MTE/QE benchmark results, training-data ablations and AfriMTE generalization experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original annotation and evaluation results, including Portuguese–Nyanja results and new encoder and filtered-data ablations.

M1.justification: v2 replaces AfroXLMR-76L with AfroXLMR-114L, developed through continued pretraining on monolingual, synthetic and Portuguese–Emakhuwa data (Section 4.2). Section 5.6 also introduces greedy sample filtering using three silver labellers for additional model variants. The underlying COMET STL, MTL and QE architectures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: SSA-MTE adds Portuguese–Nyanja, with 3,489 training, 135 development and 1,241 test examples. Emakhuwa gains training coverage, and encoder pretraining expands from 76 to 114 languages. Section 5.6 additionally reports training with filtered excluded-language data. The news-domain MTE/QE tasks and AfriMTE benchmark remain.

E2.justification: The matched MTE, QE, LLM-prompting and AfriMTE comparisons retain their baseline membership: lexical metrics, COMET22, MetricX-24, AfriCOMET variants and the same eight LLMs, as applicable. The additional encoder/filtering configurations are internal SSA-COMET ablations.

E3.justification: Table 2 changes Emakhuwa from test-only to 3,309 training and 130 development examples, retaining its 930 test examples. v2 introduces crossed 76L/114L and filtered-data controls. Appendix F also changes the stated selection threshold from 0.5 to 0.48; this establishes a reported criterion revision, not that the selected examples changed.

E4.justification: Sections 5.5–5.6 and new Table 7 test two previously unisolated questions: the effect of encoder coverage and the value of filtered data from excluded languages. Existing WMT-data ablations are updated. Error-span prompting, zero-versus-five-shot comparisons and Yorùbá qualitative examples already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report point correlations and the same annotation-agreement statistics. Neither reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The additional Nyanja agreement row follows the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added. Table 3's SSA-COMET-MTL mean changes from 0.626 across ten test pairs to 0.639 across eleven, alongside changed training and encoder settings; this is not an identical-setting gain. AfriMTE MTL Spearman/Pearson averages change from 0.507/0.589 to 0.513/0.601. Existing baseline entries also change, including AfriCOMET-v1.1-MTL's eng-luo Pearson value, 0.535 to 0.685 (v1 Table 7; v2 Table 8).

T1.justification: The regression/MSE and multi-view averaging formulations are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive mathematical definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion expand the dataset contribution from 13 pairs and over 63,000 annotations to 14 pairs and over 73,000. The introduction changes seven newly covered pairs to eight. The central claims about African evaluation resources, SSA-COMET and competitiveness with strong LLMs remain.

C2.justification: The main text removes the Emakhuwa encoder-coverage limitation and interprets the new ablations as evidence for broader pretraining and complementary filtered supervision. Other limitations, including adequacy-only evaluation, remain. Appendix I still retains the old explanation that Emakhuwa is absent from the encoder's pretraining.

D1.justification: v2 adds pretraining corpus-selection rules, an AfroXLMR-114L checkpoint link and TPU v4-8 hardware information. Appendix F newly specifies the silver labeller's encoder, eight language pairs and WMT data. Existing downstream training details and prompting templates are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ali et al. (2024b), 'Expanding FLORES+ benchmark for more low-resource settings,' as a source of Portuguese–Emakhuwa pretraining data. Section 4.2 expands the relationship to earlier AfroXLMR adaptations, while the broader related-work positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative are retained. v2 adds encoder and ablation subsections, folds the standalone Emakhuwa subsection into the dataset discussion, expands Appendix F and acknowledgments, and revises affiliations and local wording.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the language map and Emakhuwa chart, adds a Nyanja chart and Table 7, expands result tables and reverses the WMT-ablation column order. Existing appendix graphics are retained, with several resized or relocated, especially the error-span prompt. The overall visual format remains similar.

improvement.justification: The new encoder and filtering controls strengthen the experimental explanation, while Emakhuwa training resources and encoder support address a limitation identified in v1. However, integration is incomplete: Table 2 adds Emakhuwa training data while Section 5 and Appendix C still describe it as test-only, and Section 5.4 retains 0.586 although Table 6 now reports 0.609 for MTL without WMT. These reporting inconsistencies limit the overall improvement.
